title: Udasi places today
hook: Udasi centers still stand in Punjab and beyond

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Udasis: the order traced to Baba Sri Chand, who kept the lamps lit when Khalsa Sikhs could not. Your line was keepers in hard times. Who did you thank for keeping something going? Day one thousand three hundred four.

Through a low gate, there's a courtyard with a big old tree in the middle and a wide platform under it. In one corner, a fire pit with ash that someone tends every day. A low building with a painted doorway, and inside, on a raised seat, the Guru's word, wrapped in cloth. A man with long uncut hair and saffron cloth sweeps the floor before the visitors arrive. This is not a scene from an old painting. Places like this stand today. Yesterday we met the Udasis in the hard years. Today: where they still are.
screen: `A COURTYARD, A TREE, A FIRE PIT.` → `THE GURU'S WORD ON A RAISED SEAT.` → `NOT AN OLD PAINTING.`

segments.voice: Udasi centers go by a few names. A dera is a seat or settlement, a place where a teacher and his followers live. An akhara is a larger house of an order, a center with its own rules and leaders. Udasi deras and akharas still stand in Punjab, and beyond it. Tradition says Udasi teachers carried Guru Nanak's word far from Punjab, and that some of their places sit along the great rivers of north India, where they join the vast gatherings of renunciants of many orders. Others, tradition says, stand across the border, in what is now Pakistan. Second, what you'd see inside. The details differ from place to place. Udasi places are known for keeping Guru Nanak's hymns at the center and honoring Baba Sri Chand. Some also keep practices from the wider world of Indian renunciants: the ash, the fire, the saffron. So a visitor may find something that looks familiar and something that looks different, in the same courtyard. Third, the honest part. Sikhs hold a range of views about the Udasis today: some see a branch of the panth with roots in the Guru's own family, some see a separate order with its own path, and others simply honor what they kept. This path describes; it doesn't decide. And here's a line from the Japji that fits any of these places. Guru Nanak describes the earth set among nights and seasons, days and dates, wind and water, and in paraphrase, he calls it a dharamsal: a place set up for practicing what is right. Sikh tradition remembers dharamsal as an early name for a place of worship. The Japji makes the whole earth one. Udasi places are small rooms in that big one, still standing.
screen: `DERA: A SEAT. AKHARA: A HOUSE.` · `IN PUNJAB, AND BEYOND IT.` · `FAMILIAR AND DIFFERENT, ONE COURTYARD.` · `THE EARTH AS A DHARAMSAL.` · then, large: `STILL STANDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up one. That comes after the bell. For now, settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the oldest place of prayer or quiet you know: a building, a corner of a park, a grandmother's shelf. Picture who kept it standing before you ever saw it. Hands that swept the floor. Someone who lit the lamp on a day no one came. Let your breath slow. Then, when the bell rings, look up one Udasi place by name, and read one thing about it. The bell holds the time.
Udasi places today. Deras and akharas of the Udasi order, still standing in Punjab and beyond, keeping Guru Nanak's hymns and the memory of Baba Sri Chand. Today's word.
Your line: still standing. Today, notice one old place on your usual route, a shop, a church, a gurdwara, a tree, and ask who has kept it standing all this time. Day one thousand three hundred four.

howItsDone: Udasi deras and akharas still stand in Punjab and beyond; visitors find Guru Nanak's hymns honored there, alongside Baba Sri Chand's memory and renunciant customs of their own.

notes: No specific Udasi places are named. The script says, as tradition, that some Udasi centers stand along the great rivers of north India and take part in large gatherings of renunciants (the Udasin akharas at the Kumbh), and that some stand in present-day Pakistan (e.g., Sadh Belo in Sindh). Please confirm before any place is named in a later edit.
Definitions of dera (seat/settlement) and akhara (house/center of an order) are simplified; please confirm.

'Some also keep practices from the wider world of Indian renunciants: the ash, the fire, the saffron' describes dhuni fires and dress at some Udasi centers; please confirm this is fair and not overstated.

Japji pauri 34 (Ang 7): 'raatee rutee thitee vaar, pavan paanee agnee paataal, tis vich dhartee thaap rakhee dharamsaal' paraphrased. 'In Sikh speech, dharamsal was the early word for a place of worship' is a general claim; please confirm.
The range of Sikh views about the Udasis is stated without ranking; please confirm the three positions are fairly described.
